name: createClient
description:
Creates a Defjs client from option helpers.

Options apply in order: a later option overwrites an earlier one for the same setting, and interceptors accumulate. Prefer creating the client inside the request boundary when interceptors close over auth or tenants. Default HTTP/SSE fetch availability is checked when the interceptor chain invokes transport.
signatures: function createClient(...options: ClientOption[]): Client;

exampleFiles.code:
import { createClient, withEndpoint } from "@defjs/core";

const client = createClient(withEndpoint("https://api.example.com"));

returns: A client that can `execute` HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket commands.

name: withEndpoint
description:
Sets the valid absolute base URL prepended to relative request paths.

The default is an empty string, so execution requires an explicit endpoint. Its pathname is kept as a directory; its query and hash are discarded. For WebSocket commands, an `http:` base becomes `ws:` and `https:` becomes `wss:`.

A missing, relative, or invalid endpoint, or an illegal request path, fails with `REQ_BUILD_FAILED` during building, before any interceptor or transport runs, even when an interceptor would short-circuit. HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket share this rule. The resolved request must keep the base origin and stay under its directory; C0 control characters (including tab, CR, and LF), backslashes, `?`, `#`, and directory escapes in a path are rejected. Scheme-like and protocol-relative forms are rejected even with leading spaces; a plain inner space is allowed and sent as `%20`. An interceptor's final `req.endpoint` is checked against its final `req.baseEndpoint` with the same rule, but it may deliberately replace the base with another valid absolute URL. Deterministic URL errors are never retried.
signatures: function withEndpoint(endpoint: string): ClientOption;

parameters.description: Absolute base endpoint. Missing or invalid endpoints fail request building.

name: withQuerySerializer
description:
Replaces query encoding for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket requests.

`serializer(query)` receives the encoded wire object: aliases applied, `Date` as an ISO string, `bigint` as a string. Nested objects and arrays are kept as they are. It must return the query string without a leading `?`. The string is used verbatim.

It is not called when the request has no query. A builder that returns `URLSearchParams` skips it. Without this option, queries use `URLSearchParams`: arrays repeat keys and a nested object fails.

name: withXSRF
description:
Enables XSRF cookie-to-header token forwarding for HTTP requests.

SSE and WebSocket requests do not get the header. `cookieName` defaults to `XSRF-TOKEN` and `headerName` to `X-XSRF-TOKEN` when names are omitted.

- The header is set only when all of these hold: the method is not `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, or `TRACE`; the request does not already have that header; the client has an endpoint; and, whenever `location` exists (Window or Worker), the resolved request URL has the same origin as `location.origin`. A cross-origin request does not call the provider.
- Without `tokenProvider`, the token is read from `document.cookie` and URL-decoded only when `document` exists. Workers and servers need a provider to supply a token.
- With `tokenProvider`, the cookie is never read. The provider receives the request, and its result is the token. An empty string, `null`, or `undefined` means no header.

name: withSSEOnInvalidEvent
description:
Observes SSE events that have no matching event struct or fail validation.

The handler may be async and is awaited. The callback receives:

```ts
{
  reason: 'missing-struct' | 'validation-failed'
  message: { id: string; event: string; data: string }
  cause?: unknown
  signal: AbortSignal
}
```

- The invalid event is **always dropped**; it is never delivered to the stream. The callback only observes it.
- The return value is ignored. An error thrown by the callback is swallowed and does not close the stream, unless `signal` has already aborted.
- `cause` is set for `validation-failed`. Without a handler the invalid event is dropped silently.

name: withWebSocketBeforeConnect
description:
Runs a hook before the initial WebSocket connect and before every reconnect.

The hook type is:

```ts
(context: { attempt: number; signal: AbortSignal }) => void | Promise<void>
```

- `attempt` is `0` for the first connect and grows by one for each reconnect.
- Pass `signal` into token refreshes and other async work so cancelling the session stops them.
- If the hook throws, the attempt fails with an `EXT_HOOK_FAILED` fault.
- A `beforeConnect` in the execute options replaces this one for that call.

name: withWebSocketHeartbeat
description:
Enables WebSocket heartbeat messages with optional acknowledgement detection.

Passing `undefined` clears an earlier setting. The option type is:

```ts
{
  intervalMs: number
  isAck?: (message: unknown) => boolean
  message?: <T = unknown>() => T | unknown
  timeoutMs?: number
}
```

- Every `intervalMs`, `message()` is called and its result is sent through the endpoint's `outgoing` struct. No message is sent when `message` is omitted or returns `undefined`.
- With `timeoutMs`, an acknowledgement is expected after each heartbeat. `isAck` receives the decoded incoming message; when it returns `true`, the timer is cleared and that message is **not** delivered to `receive`.
- If no ack arrives within `timeoutMs`, or a heartbeat cannot be sent, the session fails. This does not trigger a reconnect.
- Heartbeat uses the same JSON guard as `session.send`: a value JSON cannot represent after struct encoding causes `TypeError` and ends the logical session.
- `intervalMs` and `timeoutMs` must be positive, finite, and at most `2_147_483_647`; otherwise execute fails with `REQ_OPTIONS_INVALID`.
- A `heartbeat` in the execute options replaces this one for that call.

parameters.description: Heartbeat interval, payload, timeout, and ACK predicate.

name: withWebSocketReconnect
description:
Configures automatic reconnection when the socket closes for any reason other than a manual `session.close()`.

Reconnection is opt-in: without this option a close ends the session. Passing `undefined` clears an earlier setting. The option type is:

```ts
{
  attempts?: number
  delayMs?: number
  factor?: number
  jitter?: number
  maxDelayMs?: number
  shouldReconnect?: (context: { attempt: number; cause?: unknown; code?: number; reason?: string; wasClean?: boolean }) => boolean
}
```

- `attempts` is the retry budget for each outage. It defaults to `3`, and `0` disables reconnection. Successful `open` resets the budget and backoff exponent; the next outage starts at retry 1. Omitting it does not give unlimited retries within one outage. A socket that successfully opens and is immediately closed again by the server can keep reconnecting at the base delay (subject to jitter and caps), because every open resets the budget; use `shouldReconnect` to stop it.
- `delayMs` defaults to `1000`, `factor` to `2`, `maxDelayMs` to `30000`, and `jitter` (0 to 1) to `0`. Retry _n_ starts with `delayMs * factor^(n-1)`, capped at `maxDelayMs`; jitter and rounding follow, then the final delay is capped again at `maxDelayMs` and `2_147_483_647` ms. A zero base stays zero; valid-number overflow saturates at those caps.
- `shouldReconnect` can return `false` to end the session instead. Without it every close is retried while the budget lasts. It is not called for a manual `session.close()`.
- Reconnect options are validated before connecting: `attempts` must be a non-negative safe integer; `delayMs` must be finite and non-negative; `maxDelayMs` must be a non-negative finite number or positive `Infinity`, which removes the configured cap but not the platform limit of `2_147_483_647` ms; `factor` must be finite and positive; `jitter` must be finite and within 0–1. Invalid values make execute fail with `REQ_OPTIONS_INVALID` before connecting. `attempts: 0` disables subsequent retries, but all explicitly supplied reconnect fields are still validated before the initial connection.
- A `reconnect` in the execute options replaces this one for that call.

name: ClientSSEOptions
description:
Optional SSE settings applied when creating a client: fetch handle, invalid-event hook, and reconnect policy.

- **handle** — Fetch implementation that opens the stream. The default resolves `globalThis.fetch` on each attempt, including replacements installed after import. Every SSE handle receives a `Request`. Missing global Fetch fails default execution with `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`; a custom handle remains usable.
- **onInvalidEvent** — Called when an event has no matching struct and no `default` struct (`'missing-struct'`), or its data fails validation (`'validation-failed'`). The event is skipped. An error thrown by the hook does not close the stream.
- **reconnect** — Opt-in. Without it the stream never reconnects. `attempts` defaults to **3** per outage; `attempts: 0` disables retry. A successful handshake resets the budget, callback `attempt`, and backoff exponent. `delayMs` is the first base delay, 1000 by default, and a server-sent `retry:` value replaces it. `factor` defaults to 1. `jitter` is a 0–1 multiplicative factor and defaults to 0. `maxDelayMs` caps the final delay after jitter and rounding; without a configured cap, the platform limit of `2_147_483_647` ms still applies. A zero base stays zero; valid-number overflow saturates at the caps. Without `shouldReconnect` only `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` reconnect; with it, its result decides for every method and its context carries `method`. A `ReadableStream` request body never reconnects. Reconnect sends the latest ID as UTF-8 bytes in `Last-Event-ID`; an empty ID clears it and an ID containing NUL is ignored.

Reconnect options are validated before interceptors or Fetch: `attempts` is a non-negative safe integer; `delayMs` must be finite and non-negative; `maxDelayMs` must be a non-negative finite number or positive `Infinity`, which removes the configured cap but not the platform limit of `2_147_483_647` ms; `factor` is finite and positive; `jitter` is finite and within 0–1. Invalid values return `REQ_OPTIONS_INVALID` at execute time.

Set these with `withSSEHandle`, `withSSEOnInvalidEvent`, and `withSSEReconnect`. Omitting `withSSEReconnect` disables retry.

name: ClientWebSocketOptions
description:
Optional WebSocket settings applied when creating a client: constructor, `beforeConnect` hook, heartbeat, protocols, and reconnect policy.

- **handle** — WebSocket constructor; defaults to `globalThis.WebSocket`.
- **beforeConnect** — Runs before each connect and reconnect attempt.
- **heartbeat** — Sends `message()` every `intervalMs`. With `timeoutMs` and `isAck`, a missing acknowledgement marks the connection unhealthy. `intervalMs` and `timeoutMs` must be positive and at most 2147483647.
- **protocols** — Subprotocols passed to the constructor.
- **reconnect** — Opt-in. `attempts` defaults to **3**; `0` disables retry, and omitting `attempts` is not unlimited. Other defaults: `delayMs` 1000, `factor` 2, `jitter` 0 (a 0-1 multiplicative factor), `maxDelayMs` 30000. `shouldReconnect` receives the close `code`, `reason`, and `wasClean` and can veto a retry.

The retry budget applies per outage. Successful `open` resets the budget, callback attempt, and backoff exponent; the next outage starts at retry 1. `maxDelayMs` caps the final delay after jitter and rounding, also bounded by `2_147_483_647` ms. See {@link withWebSocketReconnect} for validation rules and overflow behavior.

Set these with `withWebSocketHandle`, `withWebSocketBeforeConnect`, `withWebSocketHeartbeat`, `withWebSocketProtocols`, and `withWebSocketReconnect`. `WebSocketExecuteOptions` can override `beforeConnect`, `heartbeat`, `protocols`, and `reconnect` per call.

If the setter throws, it requests best-effort closure of the constructed handle before failing that attempt with `NET_UNREACHABLE`; the socket is not left outside cleanup. name: defineRequest
description:
Declares a typed HTTP request endpoint.

Pass method, path, an optional input struct, and the single `output` and
`error` structs. Call the returned endpoint with input to get an `HttpCommand`
for `client.execute`.

The contract is `method`, `path`, an optional `input` struct, optional
`output` and `error` structs, and an optional `operation`. A declared `input`
always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters;
the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without
`input` may omit `builder`. `ResponseDeclaration` and `BuilderField` are
internal helper types: `output` and `error` are required only when the
matching type parameter is a struct, and `builder` is
`(input: BuilderInput<TInput>) => HttpRequestShape` when `input` is declared.

`output` is one struct for the 2xx body; `error` is one struct for every
non-2xx body. Neither is keyed by status. A declaration is an assertion:
omitting one means that body is never read.
returns:
An endpoint that creates `HttpCommand` values from input.

The checked example file passes the whole input object as `path`. This snippet maps individual fields into `path` and `query` instead:

tags.name: example
tags.text:
```ts
const getUser = defineRequest({
  method: 'GET',
  path: '/users/:id',
  input: struct.object({ id: struct.number(), verbose: struct.boolean() }),
  builder: (input) => ({ path: { id: input.id }, query: { verbose: input.verbose } }),
  output: struct.object({ id: struct.number(), name: struct.string() }),
})
```

name: executeHttpCommand
description:
Runs an `HttpCommand` against client config: validate input, send the request, and parse the response.

Low-level entry used by `client.execute`. Prefer `client.execute(command, options)`
in application code. `HttpClientConfig` is the HTTP part of `ClientConfig`, so
a `ClientConfig` is accepted. `HttpExecuteAwaitResult` is the internal result
tuple.

The result is `[null, data, response]` or `[fault, undefined, undefined]`.
`data` is the decoded `output` body, or `undefined` when none is declared.
`response` is `DecodedResponse` when `output` is declared and `HttpMeta`
otherwise. The fault is `Fault<TError>`. A non-2xx status is `HTTP_STATUS`
when no `error` struct is declared (its `data` is `undefined`) or when the
declared body decodes (its `data` is that body). When a declared `error` body
cannot be read, the fault is a `RES_*` decode fault instead. On failure the
tuple's third slot is `undefined`; the fault carries the response metadata.
`options.timeout` falls back to the client's `withTimeout` default when omitted.

  command: HttpCommand<TInput, TOutput, TError>,
  options?: HttpExecuteOptions,
): Promise<HttpExecuteAwaitResult<TOutput, TError>>;

description:
Builds an `HttpResponse` without a network call, for interceptors that short-circuit `next` and for tests.

Default status is `0`, so pass a 2xx `status` for a success. `ok` is true for
2xx. The value it returns goes through the same media-type check and the same
declared struct as one off the wire; there is no trusted short-circuit. For a
JSON body, set a JSON `content-type` header.

name: RequestDefinition
description:
Contract for an HTTP endpoint: method, path, optional input, and the structs that decode its bodies.

Declaring `input` requires an explicit `builder` to place the parsed value on
the request. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides
where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`.
`output` declares the body for a 2xx response, `error` the body for anything
else. Only one of the two ever runs, and omitting one means that body is never
read. `ResponseDeclaration` is an internal helper type: `output` and `error`
are required only when the matching type parameter is a struct. There is no
`responseType`: the struct kind selects how a declared body is read. Pass to
`defineRequest` to get a typed endpoint.

name: RequestEndpoint
description:
Callable endpoint returned by `defineRequest`.

Call it to get an `HttpCommand`: with no arguments when the endpoint declares
no `input`, with an optional argument when the input struct accepts
`undefined`, and otherwise with the struct's input value.

name: BuilderInput
description:
Parsed endpoint input that a request builder receives.

Object nodes are intersected with the internal `Typed` brand, so they carry the struct that
produced them and alias, `Date`, and `bigint` encoding follow the value into
the request. Record entries and tuple items are branded the same way. At
runtime a record container is also tagged when the parsed value is an object,
whether or not it was merged. Array and tuple containers are not. `null` and
`undefined` are never tagged. Nullish modifiers recover the struct they
wrapped. Union options are distributed; intersection options are combined.
Any other struct falls back to `Infer<S>`.

`CarriedStruct`, `NullishBuilderInput`, `IntersectBuilderInputs`, and `Typed`
are internal helper types.
signatures:
type BuilderInput<S> =
  S extends CarriedStruct<infer Inner>
    ? NullishBuilderInput<S, Inner>
    : S extends UnionStruct<infer Options>
      ? BuilderInput<Options[number]>
      : S extends DiscriminatedUnionStruct<infer Options>
        ? BuilderInput<Options[number]>
        : S extends IntersectionStruct<infer Options>
          ? IntersectBuilderInputs<Options>
          : S extends RecordStruct<infer Value>
            ? { [key: string]: BuilderInput<Value> }
            : S extends TupleStruct<infer Items>
              ? {
                  [K in keyof Items]: Items[K] extends StructLike<
                    unknown,
                    unknown,
                    boolean
                  >
                    ? BuilderInput<Items[K]>
                    : Items[K];
                }
              : S extends ArrayStruct<infer Item>
                ? BuilderInput<Item>[]
                : S extends ObjectStruct<infer Shape>
                  ? { [K in keyof Shape]: BuilderInput<Shape[K]> } & Typed
                  : Infer<S>;

name: HttpRequestShape
description:
Request shape an HTTP builder returns: path, query, headers, and body.

`P` is the endpoint path and `M` its method. `GET` and `HEAD` cannot return a
body. `BodyValue` is a wire value Fetch sends as is (`string`, `Blob`,
`ArrayBuffer`, a typed array or `DataView`, `FormData`, `URLSearchParams`,
`ReadableStream<Uint8Array>`) or JSON data (`number`, `boolean`, `bigint`,
`Date`, `null`, an array, or an object type with string keys); an `interface`
value or class instance needs `{ ...value }`. `path` values must be scalars.
A header value may be a scalar or an array of scalars, and `HeadersInit` is
accepted. `query` may nest, and a nested object needs `withQuerySerializer`
at runtime. `FlatRecord`, `QueryRecord`, `PathValue`, and `BodyValue` are
internal helper types.

name: HttpCommand
description:
Opaque executable HTTP command produced by a `defineRequest` endpoint.

Created by calling a `RequestEndpoint` with input. It carries the request
definition and optional typed input for `client.execute`. Treat it as opaque
and pass it to `client.execute`.

name: HttpExecuteOptions
description:
Options passed to `client.execute` or `executeHttpCommand` for one HTTP call: progress, `abort` or `timeout`, and `signal`.

Cancellation is `abort` or `timeout`, not both (`abort` XOR `timeout`).
`signal` combines with either; it is not an alias for `abort`. Valid shapes:
`{ timeout }`, `{ abort }`, `{ signal, timeout }`, `{ signal, abort }`.
`{ abort, timeout }` is invalid and makes the call resolve with a
`REQ_OPTIONS_INVALID` fault. `timeout` must be a positive safe integer in
`1..2_147_483_647`.

When `timeout` is omitted, the client's `withTimeout` default applies;
`abort` combines with that default.

overloads.signature: type HttpExecuteOptions = UseRequestConfig & { signal?: AbortSignal };

name: UseRequestConfig
description:
Per-request options for HTTP execution: progress callbacks and cancellation.

The HTTP-specific part of {@link HttpExecuteOptions}, which adds `signal`.
`onDownloadProgress` and `onUploadProgress` are {@link HttpProgressFn}
callbacks. They receive an {@link HttpProgressEvent} with `loaded`, `total`,
and `lengthComputable`.

Cancellation is either `abort` or `timeout`, never both. The type rejects
both, and at runtime passing both fails with a `REQ_OPTIONS_INVALID` fault.
`timeout` must be a positive safe integer no greater than `2_147_483_647`.
It replaces the default set by {@link withTimeout} for that call. `abort`
combines with that default instead.

name: HttpRequest
description:
Normalized outgoing HTTP request seen by transports, handlers, interceptors, and `fetchHandler` after the builder runs.

`body` is already the wire value. For JSON that is a **JSON text string**;
sign HMAC or digests against that string (or other final bytes), not the
original struct input.

- `bodyContentType` holds the inferred type of the builder's body. `null` suppresses that header. FormData owns its multipart boundary. HTTP inference follows a direct write to `body` and is not copied by object spread; an explicit `bodyContentType` assignment is copied. A replacement body is detected again, so declare its type with a `content-type` header. For the unchanged body, `null` suppresses library inference when there is no explicit header, but native Fetch may add its own string type.
- HTTP never writes inferred Content-Type into `headers`; interceptors see only declared headers. An explicit `content-type` header always wins over `bodyContentType` and detection, whether set by the builder, client defaults, an interceptor, or a raw `fetchHandler` request. `body: undefined` has no library-inferred Content-Type. Signers should read `headers.get('content-type') ?? request.bodyContentType`; do not configure internal fields.
- `endpoint` is the path with path parameters filled in; `baseEndpoint` is the client endpoint.
- Interceptors see `queryParams` as `new URLSearchParams(queryString)`. A builder that returns `URLSearchParams` passes that instance through.
- `operation` is a static, low-cardinality endpoint identity for telemetry and diagnostics.
- `downloadProgress` and `uploadProgress` are the `onDownloadProgress` and `onUploadProgress` hooks of `HttpExecuteOptions`.
- `responseType` and `errorResponseType` are readonly: they are derived from the endpoint's `output` and `error` struct kinds and must not be changed. Each is set only when its struct is declared. An interceptor that short-circuits with `makeResponse` reads them to match the transport.

name: HttpResponse
description:
Wire-shape HTTP response that transports produce and interceptors accept.

`body` is parsed JSON, text, a `Blob`, or an `ArrayBuffer`, according to
`responseType`, not a decoded struct value. `body` is `undefined` when no body
was present; a JSON `null` stays `null`. For a JSON representation, a string
is a JSON string root and is not parsed again; bytes and blobs are raw and
are parsed once. `ok` is true for status codes in the 2xx range. A transport
failure is a fault, never a response. `DecodedResponse` is what reaches the
caller. The symbol key is an internal brand. Build values with `makeResponse`.

are `blob`, `arrayBuffer` is `arraybuffer` (bytes), and every other kind is

name: HttpProgressEvent
description:
Progress snapshot passed to upload and download callbacks.

Mirrors the `ProgressEvent` fields `loaded`, `total`, and `lengthComputable`.
`loaded` counts bytes read from the upload or download stream, not bytes
acknowledged by the server. Download bytes may already be decompressed.
Unknown lengths use `total: 0` and `lengthComputable: false`. A download total
is computable only with a positive `Content-Length` and an absent or
`identity` `Content-Encoding`; compressed downloads, other encoded responses,
and bytes exceeding `Content-Length` have an unknown decoded length. A
streamed FormData upload also has an unknown total unless a valid explicit
`Content-Length` supplies it. Other unknown-length streams use the same
`0` / `false` fields.

name: HttpProgressFn
description:
Callback invoked as request bytes are uploaded or response bytes are downloaded.

Passed as `onDownloadProgress` or `onUploadProgress` in `HttpExecuteOptions`.
Callbacks may be async and are awaited before the next chunk is processed. A
callback that throws or rejects fails the call with `EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`,
with the thrown value as `cause`, for downloads and uploads alike. Caller
cancellation and `timeout` still take precedence and report `NET_ABORTED` or
`NET_TIMEOUT`.

Upload progress for a `Blob`, `File`, `ArrayBuffer`, or `FormData` body is
reported only where the runtime can stream request bodies (Bun, Node). In
browsers that body is sent unchanged and `onUploadProgress` is not called. A
caller-supplied `ReadableStream` still reports progress wherever the runtime
accepts it. Download progress is unaffected.

On server runtimes, FormData with `onUploadProgress` reads its serialized
stream directly, keeps its multipart boundary, and is sent without a
library-generated `Content-Length` (chunked over HTTP/1.1), so progress,
timeout, and abort work without buffering the whole body. It reports an
unknown total unless a valid explicit `Content-Length` supplies it. For an
endpoint that requires `Content-Length`, such as some presigned upload
targets, omit `onUploadProgress`; platform Fetch then sends FormData with its
length. Non-identity encoded downloads also report `total: 0` and
`lengthComputable: false`, since `loaded` counts decoded stream bytes.
Cancellation releases the wrapped upload stream.
signatures: type HttpProgressFn = (event: HttpProgressEvent) => Promise<void> | void;

overloads.signature: type HttpProgressFn = (event: HttpProgressEvent) => Promise<void> | void;

name: MakeResponseOptions
description:
Fields accepted by `makeResponse` when building a synthetic `HttpResponse`, for example in interceptors.

`status` defaults to `0` and `statusText` to `''`. `url` and `headers` default
to values taken from `request`: its resolved URL (base endpoint, path and
query) and a copy of its headers. A request without `baseEndpoint` gives its
`endpoint` as written. Without a request, `url` is `''` and `headers` is
empty. An omitted `body` stays `undefined`; only an explicit `null` is a JSON
`null`.

name: struct
description:
Facade object for building protocol-boundary structs and parsing values with its constructors and `struct.parse`.

Prefer this object over importing the constructor functions one by one. Compose shapes with
`struct.object`, then parse with `struct.parse` or let HTTP/SSE/WebSocket
endpoints apply the same contracts at the wire boundary. `struct` is a plain object of helpers.

```ts
import { struct } from "@defjs/core";

const User = struct.object({
  id: struct.number(),
  displayName: struct.string().alias("display_name"),
});

const [error, user] = struct.parse(User, { id: 1, displayName: "Ada" });
```

### Primitives and containers

| Helper                                                                           | Role                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| {@link struct.string}()                                     | Text                                                      |
| {@link struct.number}()                                     | Number, `NaN` rejected                                    |
| {@link struct.boolean}()                                   | Boolean                                                   |
| {@link struct.bigint}()                                     | `bigint`, or a string that parses as one                  |
| {@link struct.date}()                                         | `Date`, from a `Date`, timestamp, or string               |
| {@link struct.literal}(value)                              | Exact literal                                             |
| {@link struct.null}()                                         | Only `null`                                               |
| {@link struct.any}() / unknown() ({@link struct.unknown}) | Any value except `null` and `undefined`                   |
| {@link struct.array}(item)                                   | Array of one item struct                                  |
| {@link struct.tuple}(items)                                  | Fixed-length array; `items` is one array of structs       |
| {@link struct.record}(value)                                | Plain object with string keys and one value struct        |
| {@link struct.object}(shape)                                | Plain object with fixed fields; unknown keys are stripped |
| {@link struct.or}(...options)                                   | First matching option                                     |
| {@link struct.intersection}(...structs)               | Every struct must match; object results are merged        |
| {@link struct.discriminatedUnion}(tag, options) | Object option picked by the value of the `tag` field      |
| {@link struct.enum}(values)                                   | String array, or the values of a `{ Name: value }` object |

### Body codecs and binary values

| Helper                                                                                                                         | Role                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| {@link struct.formData}(shape) / urlencoded(shape) ({@link struct.urlencoded})                     | Object struct plus a codec tag. The tag applies only when that value is the request body root               |
| {@link struct.arrayBuffer}() / blob() ({@link struct.blob}) / file() ({@link struct.file}) | Binary values. As a body root they are sent as bytes; as `output` / `error` they select that representation |
| {@link struct.string}()                                                                                   | Text. As a body root or an inbound `string` struct, the bytes stay text                                     |

### Parsing and modifiers

{@link struct.parse}(struct, value, options?) parses an unknown value and returns `[null, value]` or `[StructError, undefined]`.

Every struct has the chainable modifiers `.optional()`, `.null()` / `.nullable()`, `.nullish()`, and `.alias(name)`. See {@link StructMethods}.

typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts any value except null and undefined, without validation.

The value is returned unchanged, and nothing inside it is validated or stripped.

- Chain `.null()`, `.optional()`, or `.nullish()` to accept `null` or `undefined`.

- The output type is `any`. Prefer {@link struct.unknown}() when the caller should narrow the value.

typeTable.name: array
typeTable.description:
Struct that parses an array with one item struct.

- Parses every element with `item` and outputs a new array. A non-array fails with `invalid_type` (expected `array`).

- Parsing stops at the first failing element, and `issue.path` holds its index.

- Throws `TypeError` when `item` is not a struct.

`ArrayStruct<S>` is not exported. It is a `Struct<StructInput<S>[], Infer<S>[]>`.
typeTable.type: <S extends StructLike<unknown, unknown, boolean>>(item: S) => ArrayStruct<S>

typeTable.name: arrayBuffer
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts an ArrayBuffer.

- Accepts an `ArrayBuffer` only. Typed arrays and other views fail with `invalid_type`.

- As a body root it is sent as bytes with `application/octet-stream`.

- As an `output` or `error` struct it makes the response body be read as an `ArrayBuffer`.

typeTable.name: bigint
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a bigint or a bigint string and outputs a bigint.

- Accepts a `bigint`, or a string that `BigInt()` can parse. A `number` is rejected.

- Output is always a `bigint`; an unparsable string fails with `invalid_type`.

- When encoded for the wire, the value becomes a decimal string.

typeTable.name: blob
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a Blob.

- Accepts a `Blob` (a `File` is a `Blob`). Anything else fails with `invalid_type`.

- As a body root it is sent as is, with the blob's own type or `application/octet-stream`.

- As an `output` or `error` struct it makes the response body be read as a `Blob`.

typeTable.name: boolean
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts boolean values.

Accepts `true` and `false` only. Other values, including `'true'` and `1`, fail with `invalid_type`.

typeTable.name: date
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a Date, timestamp, or date string and outputs a Date.

- Accepts a `Date`, a millisecond timestamp, or a string. A valid `Date` is returned as the same object. A number or string is converted with `new Date(value)`.

- Output is a `Date`. A value that produces an invalid date fails with `invalid_type`.

- When encoded for the wire, the value becomes an ISO 8601 string (`toISOString()`).

typeTable.name: discriminatedUnion
typeTable.description:
Struct that picks one object struct by the value of a tag field.

```ts
const Event = struct.discriminatedUnion("kind", [
  struct.object({ kind: struct.literal("created"), id: struct.number() }),
  struct.object({ kind: struct.literal("deleted"), id: struct.number() }),
]);
```

- Every option must be an object struct whose `discriminator` field is a required {@link struct.literal}(). A missing field, a non-literal field, an optional field, or a duplicate tag value throws `TypeError` when the struct is created.

- The input must be a plain object. The tag value selects the option, and that option parses the whole object.

- A missing tag fails with `missing_key`, and an unknown tag fails with `invalid_union`. Both report the tag field's path. Other failures come from the selected option.

- With `struct.parse(..., { aliases: true })` the tag is read from the field's alias.

`RequiredDiscriminatorOptions` and `DiscriminatedUnionStruct` are not exported. The type check rejects an option whose tag field is missing or may be `undefined`.

typeTable.name: enum
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts one value from a list of strings or from the values of an object.

- With a non-empty string array, the accepted values are the array items.

- With an object, the accepted values are the object's string and number **values**, not its keys. `{ A: 'a', B: 2 }` accepts `'a'` and `2`.

- A TypeScript numeric `enum` object also accepts its member names, because the reverse mapping is part of its values.

- A value outside the set fails with `invalid_enum`. An object with no string or number value throws `TypeError` when the struct is created.

typeTable.name: file
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a File.

- Accepts a `File` only; a plain `Blob` fails with `invalid_type`.

- Use it for a field of {@link struct.formData}(), or for a raw file body.

- As an `output` or `error` struct it makes the response body be read as a blob.

typeTable.name: formData
typeTable.description:
Object struct that is encoded as multipart FormData when it is the request body.

Parses like {@link struct.object}(), and carries a `formData` codec tag.

- The tag applies only when this struct's value is the request body root. The body is then sent as `FormData` with a platform multipart boundary.

- Arrays repeat the field name, `undefined` fields are skipped, and `Blob` / `File` values are appended as files. A nested object fails the request with `REQ_BUILD_FAILED`.

- `struct.parse` ignores the tag. It does not accept a `FormData` instance, only a plain object.

typeTable.name: intersection
typeTable.description:
Struct that requires a value to satisfy every given struct.

`struct.intersection` is variadic: pass each struct as its own argument.

- Parses the input with every struct and merges the results.

- When every struct is an object struct, the output is one object with the fields of all of them. Keys that none of them declares are removed.

- When two structs produce incompatible values for the same key, it fails with `invalid_intersection`.

- Accepts `null` only when every struct accepts it, including a nested intersection marked `.null()`.

- A single struct is returned unchanged, so it keeps its own identity and type, including `.optional()` and `.null()`. Calling it with no structs throws `TypeError`, and so does a non-struct argument.

- A nonempty variadic tuple must account for that singleton. Spreading a tuple that may contain only one member infers both the singleton and multi-member results. Its object fields may therefore be optional. A tuple known to contain at least two members keeps the required intersection semantics.

`IntersectionStruct<T>` is not exported. It is a `Struct` whose input and output are the intersections of the member types.

typeTable.name: literal
typeTable.description:

- Accepts only `value`. The comparison uses `Object.is`, so any other value fails with `invalid_literal`.

- `value` must be a `boolean`, `null`, `number`, or `string`.

- Use it for the tag field of {@link struct.discriminatedUnion}().

typeTable.name: null
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts only null.

Accepts `null` only. Every other value fails with `invalid_type`. That includes `undefined` at the root or in an array or tuple; a missing object or record field reports `missing_key` instead.

This is not the `.null()` modifier. The modifier adds `null` to the values another struct accepts.

typeTable.name: number
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts number values except NaN.

- Accepts `number` values, including `Infinity`. `NaN` and non-numbers fail with `invalid_type`.

- Strings are not coerced.

typeTable.name: object
typeTable.description:
Struct that parses a plain object with a fixed set of fields.

`shape` maps field names to structs.

- Every field is **required** by default. A missing key fails with `missing_key`.

- `.optional()` and `.nullish()` allow a missing key. An absent optional field stays absent in the output.

- `.null()` / `.nullable()` allow `null`.

- `.alias(name)` sets the field's wire key. `struct.parse` reads logical keys by default; `{ aliases: true }` and HTTP JSON decoding read wire keys, and HTTP JSON encoding writes them. Parsed output uses logical keys.

- Keys that are not in `shape` are removed from the output. The output is a new object with a `null` prototype.

- The input must be a plain object. Arrays, `Map`, and class instances fail with `invalid_type` (expected `object`).

- Parsing stops at the first failing field, and `issue.path` holds its key.

- Throws `TypeError` when `shape` is not a plain object.

`ObjectShape` is `{ [key: string]: any }`; each value must be a struct.

typeTable.name: or
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a value matching any one of several structs.

`struct.or` is variadic: pass each option as its own argument.

- Tries the options in order and returns the result of the first one that parses.

- If none matches, it fails with one `invalid_union` issue at the union's own path. The issues of the individual options are not reported.

- Throws `TypeError` when an option is not a struct.

`UnionStruct<T>` is not exported. It is a `Struct` whose input and output are the unions of the option types, without `undefined`. For tagged objects prefer {@link struct.discriminatedUnion}(), which reports the issue of the selected option.

typeTable.name: parse
typeTable.description:
Parses an unknown value with a struct and returns an error-first tuple.

- **struct** is the struct to parse with. A value that is not a struct throws `TypeError`.

- **value** is the unknown input.

- **options.aliases** defaults to `false`: object keys are read by their **logical** names (`displayName`). With `true` they are read by their wire names (`display_name`), the way HTTP/JSON codecs read them. The output always uses logical names.

- **options.errorMap** is an {@link ErrorMap} that rewrites issue messages for this call only, including bigint/date conversion failures from a struct created by another Core copy. Any string, including `''`, replaces the message; only `undefined` keeps the default. Custom text is used verbatim.

- Parsing is fail-fast: it stops at the first failure, so the error holds one issue. Unknown object keys are stripped from the output, and the input is not modified.

- At most **256 nested containers** (`object`, `array`, `record`, or `tuple`) are visited along a path, counting the root container as the first. The next container fails with `invalid_type` at its logical path, with `expected: 'value nested at most 256 levels deep'`. In a union, later candidates may still succeed; if none match, the union reports `invalid_union`. Cycles through declared container fields also reach this limit; shared non-cyclic children are allowed. Union and intersection branches do not add a container level, and `any`/`unknown` values remain opaque rather than being traversed.

```ts
const [error, user] = struct.parse(User, { id: 1, displayName: "Ada" });
if (error) return console.error(error.prettify());
```

`any` and `unknown` do not traverse their values, but an intersection may recursively merge two distinct object or array values returned by those leaves. This merge shares the same 256-container budget with its enclosing logical path. Exceeding it produces `invalid_intersection` at the rejected container's logical path. Identical references are retained without traversal, including a shared cyclic value.
typeTable.type: <S extends StructLike<unknown, unknown, boolean>>(struct: S, value: unknown, options?: { aliases?: boolean; errorMap?: ErrorMap; }) => ParseResult<S["_struct"]["output"]>

typeTable.name: record
typeTable.description:

typeTable.name: tuple
typeTable.description:
Struct that parses a fixed-length array with one struct per position.

`struct.tuple` takes **one array** of structs, not separate arguments:

```ts
const Pair = struct.tuple([struct.string(), struct.number()]);
```

- Each position is parsed with the struct at the same index. The input must be an array of exactly the same length, otherwise it fails with `invalid_type` (expected `tuple of length N`).

- Passing the structs as separate arguments, `struct.tuple(a, b)`, throws a `TypeError`.

- Throws `TypeError` when an item is not a struct.

`TupleStruct<T>` is not exported. It is a `Struct` whose input and output are tuples of the item types.

```ts
const Pair = struct.tuple([struct.string(), struct.number()]);
```

- Each position is parsed with the struct at the same index. The input must be an array of exactly the same length, otherwise it fails with `invalid_type` (expected `tuple of length N`).

- Passing the structs as separate arguments, `struct.tuple(a, b)`, throws a `TypeError`.

- Throws `TypeError` when an item is not a struct.

`TupleStruct<T>` is not exported. It is a `Struct` whose input and output are tuples of the item types.

name: struct.urlencoded
description:

- `struct.parse` ignores the tag. It does not accept a `URLSearchParams` instance, only a plain object.

name: StructError
description:
Error returned by a failed struct parse, aggregating one or more {@link StructIssue}s and their formatters.

`name` is `'StructError'`. Construct it with `constructor(issues: StructIssue[])`. `issues` is the `readonly` list of those issues. `message` is the issue's message for a single issue, `N struct issues: <first message>` for several, and `Struct parse failed` for none.

Default issue messages name the received kind and omit the value, so `message` and `prettify()` can be logged. For example, `Expected number at id, received string`. `message` and the formatters use that text. The raw value stays on `StructIssue.received`; custom `errorMap` text is used verbatim and can reintroduce sensitive values.

Use `format()`, `flatten()`, or `prettify()` to present issues to callers.

- `struct.parse` stops at the first failure, so `issues` holds one {@link StructIssue} there.

- `format()` returns a {@link FormattedStructError} tree. Each node has an `_errors` array, and nested keys follow `issue.path`.

- `flatten()` returns a {@link FlattenedStructError}: messages with an empty path go to `formErrors`, the others are grouped by the first path segment in `fieldErrors`.

- `prettify()` returns one `× path: message` line per issue. An empty path is shown as `<root>`.

- `path` runs from the parse root to the failing location: field names and array indices. It is empty for a root-level failure.

name: FaultCode
description:
Every failure Defjs reports, as one closed set of codes.

The prefix before the first `_` is the class; there is no separate `kind` field.
Read the prefix for coarse triage and the whole code for an exact case:

| Class  | Meaning                                                        |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `HTTP` | The peer answered with a non-2xx status.                        |
| `REQ`  | The request never left: input, execute options, or build.       |
| `NET`  | No usable response: cancel, timeout, connect, truncated body.   |
| `RES`  | A response arrived but could not be read as declared.           |
| `EXT`  | Code you attached to the pipeline threw.                        |
| `CAP`  | A declared buffer or queue limit was exceeded.                  |
| `ENV`  | The host runtime lacks a required capability.                   |

The set is closed on purpose: it keeps `switch (fault.code)` exhaustive. Extensions
report their own detail through `cause`, not through a new code.

name: Fault
description:
Union of every failure `client.execute` can return, discriminated by `code`.

`Fault<TErr>` is {@link FaultOf} applied to the decoded body type, so it is the
union of {@link DecodeFault}, {@link HttpStatusFault}<TErr>, and
{@link PreflightFault}. `ErrorBody<TErr>` is `undefined` when `TErr` is
`undefined`, and `Infer<TErr>` otherwise. Switch on `fault.code`.

Every variant is a native `Error` named `DefjsFault`, so `String(fault)` produces
`DefjsFault: <message>`. `code` and the variant metadata — `status`, `response`,
`data` — are enumerable own properties. The native `cause` chain is non-enumerable.

Default Struct messages say `received <kind>`, never the received value. A JSON
`SyntaxError` behind `RES_DECODE_FAILED` gives the message
`Response body could not be decoded`. Structural paths retain record keys, which
may be sensitive. Raw `StructIssue.received` and parser causes remain sensitive;
custom `errorMap` and extension messages are used verbatim and need review before
logging.

Call `format()`, `flatten()`, or `prettify()` only after narrowing `fault.cause`
to `StructError`; those helpers are not copied onto the fault.

parser failure for an unreadable representation).

body that truncated mid-download.

description:

`next(req)` only goes inward: the interceptors registered after this one, then
the Fetch handler. It is not a re-dispatch of `client.execute` from the
outside of the chain. Call `next` again for a safe

do not run a second time. Once the chain has settled, calling `next` rejects

`createWebSocketInterceptor` to register it through `withInterceptors`.

The chain runs once per `execute`. Reconnects happen inside the session it
returns and do not run it again.

name: WebSocketHandler
description:
Terminal `next` function a WebSocket interceptor receives; it opens a session for the request.

`next(req)` goes inward only: through the interceptors registered after this
one, then the transport that opens the session. It resolves to a
{@link WebSocketSessionLike}. It may be called once per execute; a second
call, or a call after the chain has settled, rejects.

name: WebSocketSessionLike
description:

type, which avoids a circular dependency between interceptors and WebSocket.

`[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` teardown as its `close` / `closed` lifecycle;
returning an unrelated resolved promise is not sufficient. Requiring this
member is a compile-time breaking change for structural implementations. Code
that only accepts sessions returned by Defjs has no additional runtime call
requirement.

description:
Opaque executable SSE command produced by an `EventStreamEndpoint`.

Created by calling an `EventStreamEndpoint` with input. It also has internal symbol-keyed members that identify and run the command. Treat it as opaque and pass it to `client.execute`. `endpoint` is the definition plus `method`, which is always a string (it defaults to `'GET'` when the definition omits it). `ResolvedEventStreamDefinition` names that shape and is not exported.

name: EventStreamExecuteOptions
description:
Per-call options for opening an SSE stream: abort or timeout, plus an optional signal.

Cancellation is `abort` **or** `timeout`, not both; passing both makes the call resolve with a `REQ_OPTIONS_INVALID` fault. `signal` combines with either and is not an alias for `abort`. `timeout` must be a positive safe integer up to 2147483647.

For SSE, `timeout` is a startup deadline. It covers input parsing, the builder, the interceptors, and opening the connection, and stops applying once the stream is open. The client-level `withTimeout` default does not apply to SSE.

- On failure: `[fault, undefined, open]`. `open` carries the response snapshot when the failure happened after a response arrived, for example a non-2xx handshake, and is `undefined` otherwise.

- `TError` is the declared `error` struct. It types the decoded error body on the fault.

name: WebSocketDefinition
description:
Contract object passed to defineWebSocket.

- `incoming` is the struct every received frame is parsed with. Frames are JSON text.

- `outgoing` is the struct `session.send` validates and encodes with. Without it, `send` throws.

- `maxIncomingQueueSize` is required and must be a positive safe integer. `maxOutgoingQueueSize` must be a non-negative safe integer; it defaults to `0`, which disables queueing of messages sent while the session is `reconnecting`.

- `protocols` is the static default subprotocol list. The `protocols` execute option and {@link withWebSocketProtocols} override it.

- `operation` is a static, low-cardinality name for telemetry.

- `input` is the struct for the command input. A declared `input` always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`. The builder may return `path` and `query` only; see {@link WebSocketRequestShape}.

Invalid queue limits are reported when the command executes, as a `REQ_OPTIONS_INVALID` fault.

- `input` accepts `undefined`: `(input?: StructInput<TInput>) => WebSocketCommand`.

- Otherwise: `(input: StructInput<TInput>) => WebSocketCommand`.

- `query` is a `URLSearchParams` or a record of scalars, arrays, and nested records.
- `headers` and `body` are `never`. A WebSocket handshake takes neither from the builder; put credentials in `beforeConnect` or an interceptor.

name: WebSocketSession
description:
Typed WebSocket session: send and receive messages, observe state, and close.

- `state` is the logical {@link WebSocketState}; `connection` is the latest {@link WebSocketConnectionInfo}. `bufferedAmount` is the native unsent byte count, or `0` with no physical socket.

- `receive` yields incoming messages already parsed with the `incoming` struct. It is one-consumer: asking for a second iterator throws a `TypeError`. A frame that cannot be parsed is reported to `onRuntimeError` listeners and skipped.

- `send(message)` validates and encodes the message with the `outgoing` struct, then sends JSON text. It sends immediately while `open`, queues while `reconnecting` when `maxOutgoingQueueSize` allows, and throws a `DOMException` named `InvalidStateError` when the session is not writable. It also throws when no `outgoing` struct is declared, the message fails the struct, or the queue is disabled or full.

- After encoding, a value JSON cannot faithfully represent throws `TypeError` before sending or entering the queue. This includes non-finite numbers, functions, symbols, `Map`, `Set`, streams, and class instances without a JSON representation, at the root or nested. The same guard protects heartbeat messages; a heartbeat serialization failure ends the session. Struct validation may reject a value first.

- `close(code?, reason?)` requests closure and stops the heartbeat. `code` must be `1000` or in `3000..4999`, and `reason` at most 123 UTF-8 bytes; invalid arguments throw before the state changes.

- `closed` resolves with the logical terminal {@link WebSocketCloseInfo}.

- `onStateChange` and `onRuntimeError` return an unsubscribe function.

Prefer `await using ownedSession = session` for owned scope cleanup. Manual `session.close()` and `await session.closed` remain available.

```ts
async function consume(
  session: WebSocketSession<unknown, never>,
): Promise<void> {
  await using ownedSession = session;
  for await (const message of ownedSession.receive) console.log(message);
}
```

The async disposer requests native close and waits for Defjs-owned teardown, but it bounds a missing close event at one second and may reject with a `DOMException` named `TimeoutError`. It cannot prove that the physical TCP connection closed.

description:

| `connecting`   | Preparing and opening the first connection                             |
| `open`         | The physical socket is open                                            |
| `reconnecting` | Preparing or waiting for a replacement socket after a close            |
| `closing`      | Closure was requested with `session.close()` or disposal               |
| `closed`       | Terminal: the session ended without an error or cancellation           |
| `aborted`      | Terminal: the session was cancelled through `abort` or `signal`        |
| `error`        | Terminal: the session failed, including a startup failure or `timeout` |

Observe it with `session.state` and `session.onStateChange`.

name: WebSocketConnectionInfo
description:
Connection metadata for the current WebSocket generation.

- `url` is the URL the socket reports.

- `protocol` is the negotiated subprotocol and `extensions` the negotiated extensions. Both are `undefined` when the socket reports an empty string.

- `generation` counts the physical sockets that reached `open`: `1` after the first open, one more after each reconnect. A snapshot taken before any open has `0`.

`session.connection` exposes the session's current public connection info. The `connection` in the execute result preserves the first successful snapshot only for a native Defjs session or a wrapper forwarding the same live `connection` object. Custom sessions and wrappers that transform `connection` instead return their current public `connection`. Sharing `closed` cannot bypass URL sanitization or metadata filtering, and Defjs does not reconstruct first-connection metadata from arbitrary transformations.

name: WebSocketCloseInfo
description:
Logical terminal outcome of a WebSocket session.

What `session.closed` resolves with, once the session has ended for good.

- `closed`: the session ended normally, including a manual `session.close()`.

- `aborted`: the session was cancelled; `cause` is the abort reason.

- `error`: the session failed; `cause` is required.

- `code`, `reason`, and `wasClean` come from the native close event when one was observed. A manual `session.close(code, reason)` fills `code` and `reason` when the close event does not.

name: ManualSocketCloseReason
description:
Close code and reason recorded when a session is closed with session.close.

Records the `code` and `reason` passed to `session.close(code?, reason?)`. They fill `code` and `reason` of the final `{ kind: 'closed' }` close info when the peer's close event carries none. `close` throws a `DOMException` when a provided `code` is not the integer `1000` or an integer from `3000` through `4999`, and when `reason` exceeds 123 UTF-8 bytes. Omitting `code` is allowed.

name: WebSocketHeartbeatConfig
description:
Heartbeat ping and acknowledgement settings for a live WebSocket session.

- `intervalMs` is the delay between heartbeat messages.

- `message()` builds the payload. It is sent through the `outgoing` struct. Nothing is sent when it is omitted or returns `undefined`.

- After struct encoding, non-JSON values fail with `TypeError` through the same serializer as `session.send`; that heartbeat failure ends the logical session without reconnecting.

- `isAck(message)` receives each decoded incoming message. When it returns `true`, the message is treated as the acknowledgement and is not delivered to `receive`.

- `timeoutMs` is how long to wait for an acknowledgement after a heartbeat. Missing it fails the session.

- `intervalMs` and `timeoutMs` must be positive, finite, and at most `2_147_483_647`.

Set it with {@link withWebSocketHeartbeat} or the `heartbeat` execute option.

name: withOpenTelemetryServer
description:
Client option that installs outbound OpenTelemetry interceptors for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket.

Appends one interceptor per enabled transport, in the order HTTP, SSE, WebSocket. Apply it at `createClient` time. It does not initialize the OpenTelemetry SDK or acquire global tracer, meter, or logger handles: pass the ones your application owns. Each transport can be toggled or customized via `http`, `sse`, and `webSocket`.

`options` is required. It carries `tracer`, `meter`, `logger`, `propagator`, `requireParentSpan`, and the `http` / `sse` / `webSocket` transport options. Pass `{}` to install the interceptors with propagation only.

Each of `tracer`, `meter` and `logger` is optional and works without the others. Without `tracer`, the plugin creates no local spans, never calls `trace.getTracer(...)`, and skips `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook`. Propagation still forwards the extracted parent context.

HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket are on by default. Pass `{ enabled: false }` on a transport to skip it.

- `tracer` — Optional. Without it there are no local spans and no span hooks.

- `meter` — Optional. Without it no package metrics are recorded.

- `logger` — Optional. A `Logger` from `@opentelemetry/api-logs`, not a Winston/Pino Logger. Without it no diagnostic LogRecords are emitted. Defjs never obtains a global logger or owns its provider.

- `propagator` — Defaults to W3C Trace Context + Baggage.

- `requireParentSpan` — Defaults to `false`. With a `tracer`, `true` bypasses all instrumentation, including logs, when no active parent span exists. Without a `tracer` it blocks neither metrics nor logs.

- `http`, `sse`, `webSocket` — Per-transport options. Each defaults to `{}`; a transport is disabled only by `{ enabled: false }`.

name: OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions
description:
Shared per-transport OpenTelemetry client options: whether the transport is enabled and its span hooks, generic over the response type.

`TResponse` is what `responseHook` receives: `HttpResponse<unknown>` for HTTP, `EventStreamHandle<unknown>` for SSE, `WebSocketSessionLike` for WebSocket. See {@link OpenTelemetryServerHttpOptions}, {@link OpenTelemetryServerSSEOptions} and {@link OpenTelemetryServerWebSocketOptions}.

`enabled` defaults to `true`; only `enabled: false` turns the transport off. The old boolean switch (`http: false`) and top-level hooks are rejected by the TypeScript types only. There is no runtime check, so at runtime `http: false` leaves the transport enabled and a top-level hook is silently ignored.

Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied. `startSpanHook` runs synchronously before span creation for its own transport. Its attributes are applied after built-in attributes, so the application may override `url.full` or another initial value. If it throws, Defjs creates the span with built-in attributes and continues the request. `requestHook` runs after span creation and before the request is sent; `responseHook` runs after the transport result is returned. Both may return a promise, but neither is awaited: a throw or rejection never blocks or fails the operation. `responseHook` receives the original request as its third argument.

While `span.isRecording()` is true, hook failures record `defjs.otel.hook.error` and `exception` events. For non-recording spans (ended or unsampled), failures go to the OpenTelemetry diagnostic logger through `diag.error`. Applications must configure `diag.setLogger(...)` from `@opentelemetry/api` to receive them; there is no automatic output by default. The package does not initialize the SDK, and this diagnostic is not a separate SDK `LogRecord`.

By default, `url.full` resolves only `request.endpoint` against optional `request.baseEndpoint`; an independent `request.queryString` is not appended. That boundary is not redaction, and the package has no built-in redactor or sensitive-key policy. Construct and, if needed, redact an application-owned URL explicitly.

description:
Options for the HTTP transport — the shared options with an HttpResponse in responseHook.

Set on `http` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. It has no fields of its own: `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`.

- `responseHook(span, res, req)` receives the `HttpResponse` that came back through the interceptor, before the client decodes a declared body, together with the original `HttpRequest`. Read `req.operation` for the request identity; do not rebuild it from the endpoint or a resolved URL.

- The HTTP span ends as soon as `responseHook` returns; the hook is not awaited, so only its synchronous part can still change the span. A status of 400 or above ends it `ERROR` with `error.type` set to the status string; 100–399 leaves its status unset. An asynchronous hook rejection after end is reported through `diag.error`; configure `diag.setLogger(...)` from `@opentelemetry/api` to receive it. It cannot append events to an ended span.

- A rejection through the interceptor has no response status and does not call `responseHook`. That includes a network failure, cancellation, timeout, any declared-body read failure (`BodyFailure`, including text, blob, and bytes, not only JSON), and a progress observer failure (`EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`). The span ends `ERROR` with `error.type` set to the thrown class name, such as `TypeError`, `Error` or `BodyFailure`. Caller cancellation is `Error` whatever the abort reason.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip HTTP instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

name: OpenTelemetryServerSSEOptions
description:
Options for the SSE transport — the shared options with the stream handle in responseHook.

Set on `sse` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. It has no fields of its own: `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`.

- `responseHook(span, stream, req)` runs once the stream has opened, before the span records `sse.connected`. `stream` is the `EventStreamHandle` the transport returned; `req` is the original `HttpRequest`.

- SSE is traced at connection level. After startup the span stays open until `stream.closed` settles, and records `sse.connected`, then one of `sse.closed` (server EOF), `sse.aborted` (`stream.close()` or a non-timeout caller abort of the open stream; the span still ends without error), or `sse.error` (including a timeout-shaped abort, which ends the span `ERROR`). No per-event spans are created.

- A non-2xx handshake is observed as a connection failure: the span ends `ERROR` and, with a `logger`, one `WARN` is emitted whatever the response body.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip SSE instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

name: OpenTelemetryServerWebSocketOptions
description:
Options for the WebSocket transport — the shared options plus queryPropagation.

Set on `webSocket` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`; `responseHook(span, session, req)` receives the opened `WebSocketSessionLike` and the original `HttpRequest`.

`queryPropagation` defaults to `false`: the WebSocket query string is left unchanged and no trace context or baggage is written into the URL. Browser WebSocket clients usually cannot set headers, so enabling it writes the propagated context to the end of the query string, replacing any parameter of the same name. Query strings can be recorded by proxies, access logs and APM tools, and baggage values can be sensitive. Turn it on only after you accept that exposure.

WebSocket is traced at connection level. The span stays open until `session.closed` settles. It records `websocket.connected`, then `websocket.closed` for a normal close or `websocket.error`. A close frame from the server counts as normal with any code, including 1011. An abrupt drop without a close frame (1006) is normal only where the runtime reports no socket `error` before `close` (Bun); where it does (Node.js), the session ends in error and logs once. A caller abort of an open session is also `websocket.error`: the span ends `ERROR` and no log is emitted. `error.type` follows the abort reason: `AbortError` for a default `abort()`, the `Error.name` of an `Error` reason, `string` for a string reason. An abort while the WebSocket is still connecting ends the span `ERROR` with `error.type` `DefjsFault`. No per-message spans are created.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip WebSocket instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

name: createResolvedRequestUrl
description:
Resolves a relative definition path under the base endpoint's origin and directory into a URL.

During `client.execute`, a missing, relative, or invalid base or an illegal
path becomes `REQ_BUILD_FAILED` before any interceptor or transport runs,
including a short-circuiting interceptor, for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket alike.
An interceptor's final `req.endpoint` is also validated against its final
`req.baseEndpoint`; deliberately replacing the base with another valid
absolute URL is allowed. Deterministic URL errors are never retried.
throws: TypeError when the endpoint or path is invalid.

parameters.name: baseEndpoint
parameters.description: A valid absolute client endpoint. Its query and hash are dropped, and a trailing slash is added to its pathname so that the base path is kept: `https://api.example.com/v1` with `/users` gives `https://api.example.com/v1/users`.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: A relative endpoint path. A single leading slash is removed. After resolution, the URL must keep the base origin and stay under its directory. Absolute or protocol-relative paths, C0 control characters (including tab, CR, and LF), backslashes, `?`, `#`, and directory escapes are rejected. Scheme-like and protocol-relative forms are rejected even with leading spaces; a plain inner space is allowed and sent as `%20`.

parameters.name: queryString
parameters.description: Query without a leading `?`. When non-empty it is set as the URL's search verbatim.

name: STRUCT
description:
Type-only export of the internal enumerable tag key on objects produced while parsing endpoint input, used by the outbound encoder.

`STRUCT` is exported as a **type** only (`export type { STRUCT }`). `@defjs/core` has no runtime `STRUCT` export, so `import { STRUCT } from '@defjs/core'` fails to compile and gives no value.

It marks those objects so the outbound encoder knows which struct produced them. Response decoding and `struct.parse` leave it unset. The symbol is internal to the outbound encoder; application code should not depend on it.
